title: Needle, meet haystack
briefing: "We're seeing a flood of failed logins on workstation.
Someone is guessing passwords. Which account are they after?"
tips: `grep WORD FILE` prints only the lines that contain WORD.
A pipe `|` feeds one command's output into the next: grep something file | tail
objective: Find the account under attack (the name with repeated failed passwords in /var/log/auth.log) and write just that name into ~/intruder.txt.
expert_objective: Brute force in progress on workstation. Identify the targeted account; its name goes in ~/intruder.txt.
hints: Don't read 3,000 lines. Filter: you only care about lines that mention failed passwords.
`grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log` keeps only those lines. Pipe it into `tail` to tame the output: which name keeps coming back?
The name comes right after 'for'. Once you know it: `echo NAME > ~/intruder.txt`.
solution:
grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | grep -o "for [a-z]*" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
echo mallory > ~/intruder.txt

reactions.say: That's... a lot of text. There's a command that keeps only the lines matching a pattern.
~/intruder.txt exists, but it doesn't hold the right answer (just the name, nothing else). `cat ~/intruder.txt` to check it.

explanation:
`grep` keeps matching lines and `|` pipes them into the next tool. The pro one-liner for 'who is attacked most?':
  grep 'Failed password' auth.log | grep -o 'for [a-z]*' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
sort groups identical lines, uniq -c counts each group, sort -rn puts the biggest first. You will use this shape for the rest of your career.
